'''Winfried Denk''' (born November 12, 1957, in Munich) is a German physicist. He built the first [[Two-photon excitation microscopy|two-photon microscope]] while he was a graduate student (and briefly a postdoc) in [[Watt W. Webb]]'s lab at [[Cornell University]], in 1989.

==Early life and education==
Denk was born in Munich, Germany. As a child he spent most of his playtime learning to use the tools and building materials in his father's workshop. In school, it became apparent that Denk’s ‘talents were unevenly spread across subjects, math and physics being favored’.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://kavliprize.org/prizes-and-laureates/laureates/winfried-denk |title=Kavli biosketch|date=20 March 2014|publisher=The Kavli Prize |access-date=2020-06-27}}</ref> Fixing and constructing electronic devices was his main hobby throughout high school.

After high school, Denk completed the mandatory 15-month stint in the German army and spent the next 3 years at [[LMU Munich]]. In 1981, he moved to [[Zurich]] to study at [[ETH Zurich]]. During this time, he also worked in the lab of Dieter Pohl, at the [[IBM Research|IBM laboratory]]. There he built one of the first [[Super-resolution microscopy|super-resolution microscopes]] and developed a passion for scanning microscopy. He did his master's thesis in the lab of [[Kurt Wüthrich]], under the direct guidance of [[Gerhard Wagner (physicist)|Gerhard Wagner]]. But he felt that NMR spectroscopy was not for him because it did not involve enough opportunities to create new experimental gadgets.

In 1984, Denk joined the lab of [[Watt W. Webb]] at Cornell. While Webb himself was extremely interested in methods – both fluorescence-correlation and photo bleaching-recovery spectroscopy had been invented in his lab – he gave students and postdocs a lot of freedom. Denk enjoyed his time at Cornell but was almost fired after he went to Greece for six weeks to study monk seals. Given a second chance, he started a project aimed at measuring the motion of sensory hair-bundles in the inner ear. One of the attractions of this endeavor was that it required a stay in San Francisco, in order to learn from [[A. James Hudspeth|Jim Hudspeth]] and his group about hair-cells in general and specifically how to prepare them for the planned measurements.

Denk returned to Cornell and invented a method sensitive enough to measure the thermal movement of hair-bundles. He went on to show that hair cells can sense their own [[Brownian motion]].<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Denk|first1=W.|last2=Webb|first2=W. W.|last3=Hudspeth|first3=A. J.|date=1989-07-01|title=Mechanical properties of sensory hair bundles are reflected in their Brownian motion measured with a laser differential interferometer.|journal=Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences|language=en|volume=86|issue=14|pages=5371–5375|doi=10.1073/pnas.86.14.5371|pmid=2787510|pmc=297624|bibcode=1989PNAS...86.5371D|issn=0027-8424|doi-access=free}}</ref>

Central to Denk's early career was his intuition that two-photon (2p) imaging might damage the sample less than one-photon confocal imaging.<ref name=":0">{{Cite journal|last1=Denk|first1=W|last2=Strickler|first2=J.|last3=Webb|first3=W.|date=1990-04-06|title=Two-photon laser scanning fluorescence microscopy|url=https://www.science.org/doi/10.1126/science.2321027|journal=Science|language=en|volume=248|issue=4951|pages=73–76|doi=10.1126/science.2321027|pmid=2321027|bibcode=1990Sci...248...73D|issn=0036-8075|url-access=subscription}}</ref> He predicted this in spite of the fact that peak light intensity for 2p is almost one million times higher than for the confocal microscope. Equally important was his insight that infrared 2p excitation would allow scattered fluorescence to contribute to images even deep in turbid samples, improving the optical access and resolution of 2p imaging over what was possible using confocal imaging.<ref name=":1">{{Cite journal|last=Denk|first=W.|date=1994-07-05|title=Two-photon scanning photochemical microscopy: mapping ligand-gated ion channel distributions.|journal=Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences|language=en|volume=91|issue=14|pages=6629–6633|doi=10.1073/pnas.91.14.6629|issn=0027-8424|pmc=44256|pmid=7517555|bibcode=1994PNAS...91.6629D|doi-access=free}}</ref>

Nowhere has this proven more valuable than when imaging neurons in living brain tissue. Two-photon microscopy remains the only technique that allows the recording of activity in living brains with high spatial resolution. 2p excitation can also be used to map cells' receptor distributions by releasing substances from their chemical "cages".<ref name=":1" />

Denk later demonstrated that 2p can be utilized to record activity in the visually stimulated retina.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Denk|first1=W.|last2=Detwiler|first2=P. B.|date=1999-06-08|title=Optical recording of light-evoked calcium signals in the functionally intact retina|journal=Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences|language=en|volume=96|issue=12|pages=7035–7040|doi=10.1073/pnas.96.12.7035|pmid=10359834|pmc=22046|bibcode=1999PNAS...96.7035D|issn=0027-8424|doi-access=free}}</ref> He also showed that it can be combined with adaptive optics to improve resolution, and with amplified pulses to push the depth limit to 1mm in brain tissue.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Rueckel|first1=M.|last2=Mack-Bucher|first2=J. A.|last3=Denk|first3=W.|date=2006-11-14|title=Adaptive wavefront correction in two-photon microscopy using coherence-gated wavefront sensing|journal=Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences|language=en|volume=103|issue=46|pages=17137–17142|doi=10.1073/pnas.0604791103|pmid=17088565|pmc=1634839|bibcode=2006PNAS..10317137R|issn=0027-8424|doi-access=free}}</ref><ref name=":2">{{Cite journal|last1=Helmchen|first1=Fritjof|last2=Denk|first2=Winfried|date=2005|title=Deep tissue two-photon microscopy|url=http://www.nature.com/articles/nmeth818|journal=Nature Methods|language=en|volume=2|issue=12|pages=932–940|doi=10.1038/nmeth818|pmid=16299478|s2cid=3339971|issn=1548-7091|url-access=subscription}}</ref> Today, two-photon excitation microscopy is also used in the fields of physiology, embryology and tissue engineering, as well as in cancer research.

The sparsity of data on connectivity between neurons had been a major limitation in circuit neuroscience. Denk’s 2004 paper<ref name=":3">{{Cite journal|last1=Denk|first1=Winfried|last2=Horstmann|first2=Heinz|date=2004-10-19|title=Serial Block-Face Scanning Electron Microscopy to Reconstruct Three-Dimensional Tissue Nanostructure|url= |journal=PLOS Biology|volume=2|issue=11|pages=e329|doi=10.1371/journal.pbio.0020329|pmid=15514700|pmc=524270|issn=1545-7885 |doi-access=free }}</ref> describing automated [[Serial Block-Face Scanning Electron Microscopy|serial blockface microscopy]] rekindled the dormant science of comprehensive neural circuit mapping ([[connectomics]]), pioneered by Sydney Brenner.<ref>{{Cite journal|date=1986-11-12|title=The structure of the nervous system of the nematode Caenorhabditis elegans|url=https://royalsocietypublishing.org/doi/10.1098/rstb.1986.0056|journal=Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society of London. B, Biological Sciences|language=en|volume=314|issue=1165|pages=1–340|doi=10.1098/rstb.1986.0056|pmid=22462104|issn=0080-4622|last1=White|first1=J. G.|last2=Southgate|first2=E.|last3=Thomson|first3=J. N.|last4=Brenner|first4=S.|bibcode=1986RSPTB.314....1W|url-access=subscription}}</ref>

Denk was Director at the [[Max Planck Institute for Biological Intelligence]] (formerly [[Max Planck Institute of Neurobiology]]<ref>{{cite web |title=New Max Planck Institute for Biological Intelligence |url=https://idw-online.de/en/news788973 |access-date=2022-04-20}}</ref>) and retired in 2025.<ref>{{cite web |title=Former Directors (MPIN, MPIO, MPIV, MPI-BI) |url=https://www.bi.mpg.de/formers |access-date=2026-01-28}}</ref> He continues working to improve techniques for circuit-mapping in the rodent brain.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Mikula|first1=Shawn|last2=Denk|first2=Winfried|date=2015|title=High-resolution whole-brain staining for electron microscopic circuit reconstruction|url=http://www.nature.com/articles/nmeth.3361|journal=Nature Methods|language=en|volume=12|issue=6|pages=541–546|doi=10.1038/nmeth.3361|pmid=25867849|s2cid=8524835|issn=1548-7091|url-access=subscription}}</ref> His most recent work involves precisely determining the positions, orientations, and identities of proteins and bound ligands in cryo-preserved cells.<ref>{{Cite bioRxiv |last1=Rickgauer|first1=J. Peter|last2=Choi|first2=Heejun|last3=Lippincott-Schwartz|first3=Jennifer|last4=Denk|first4=Winfried|date=2020-04-24|title=Label-free single-instance protein detection in vitrified cells|biorxiv=10.1101/2020.04.22.053868}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Rickgauer|first1=J Peter|last2=Grigorieff|first2=Nikolaus|last3=Denk|first3=Winfried|date=2017-05-03|title=Single-protein detection in crowded molecular environments in cryo-EM images|journal=eLife|language=en|volume=6|article-number=e25648|doi=10.7554/eLife.25648|issn=2050-084X|pmc=5453696|pmid=28467302 |doi-access=free }}</ref>
